# Alfred North Whitehead
Alfred North Whitehead (1861–1947) was a prominent mathematician and philosopher best known for his development of "process philosophy," often termed the "philosophy of organism." Rejecting the classical view of reality as composed of static, unchanging bits of matter, Whitehead proposed that reality is fundamentally constituted by interrelated events and processes of "becoming." He argued that all entities, from electrons to human beings, possess some degree of experience or "prehension," a mode of perception that incorporates aspects of the past and environment into the present. This panexperientialist view, which he distinguished from panpsychism, posits that creativity is the absolute principle of existence, driving the novelty and freedom inherent in every actual occasion.
Whitehead's intellectual legacy is significant yet complex; while his work was highly influential in the fields of theology (specifically process theology), ecology, and education, it remained relatively obscure in mainstream analytic philosophy due to the difficulty and density of his prose. Key works such as *Principia Mathematica* (co-authored with Bertrand Russell) and *Process and Reality* challenged Western assumptions about logic, mathematics, and the nature of God, introducing a "dipolar" conception of God as both a source of eternal possibilities and a being affected by the world. His educational philosophy emphasized transdisciplinary learning, the cultivation of imagination, and the rejection of "inert ideas," advocating for an education that connects knowledge to real-life values and applications. Despite being considered by some as one of the greatest 20th-century philosophers, his influence has historically been concentrated in specialized circles, particularly within American progressive theology and constructive post-modern thought.
